inline.s: Edified by these auspicious signs — our mother’s foreknowledge of the hour of her passing, her peaceful end, the warmth at the crown of her head, her body staying soft as in life, and the rest — several dozen relatives and friends who had not believed in the Buddha all knelt down and joined in the recitation of the Buddha’s name; many have already of their own accord made offerings to the Buddha and come to believe!
Truly, by the extraordinary grace of the Three Jewels, our mother’s great vow — to manifest auspicious signs throughout her life and thereby save others — has been brought to fulfillment!
Respectfully recounted by Ma Xiuxian, Xiukun, Xiuxia (holder of the five precepts), Xiufen, Xiufang, and Shichao (holder of the three refuges), and others.
(Original title: The Xu Family’s Grand-Aunt Goes to the Pure Land Carrying an Umbrella)

My family lives in Shangyang Village, Dongtianmu Township, Lin’an County, Zhejiang Province. Our neighbor Auntie Xu had a grand-aunt in her household who was devout in her faith in the Buddha. Whenever she went to a monastery to worship the Buddha, whether the weather was clear or rainy, she would always carry an umbrella and place it beneath the Buddha’s seat; after worshipping and burning incense, she would carry the umbrella home with her and keep it in a clean place in the house. When her time came, she was free of illness and pain, reciting the Buddha’s name single-mindedly without pause. Suddenly thunder rolled and rain poured down in torrents, yet within the house the light was golden and radiant, and the grand-aunt passed away peacefully amid the sound of the Buddha’s name. But the thunder would not abate, nor would the rain cease. Then the family remembered the umbrella the grand-aunt had carried on her pilgrimages to the mountains, and in haste they placed it before the old woman’s spirit tablet and burned it. A wonder occurred: the umbrella was burned entirely to ash, yet its whole form remained unbroken; suddenly there came a report, a gust of wind blew the umbrella upright, and slowly at first, then swiftly, it drifted westward with the whirlwind. Everyone said that the old lady had gone to the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss carrying her umbrella.

blocks.text: A Report Sent Back After Rebirth in the West

inline.s: Layman Zhu Dingyi, courtesy name Jingchen, also known by the courtesy name Xingwu, was a man of Kunming in Yunnan. He practiced medicine, and in his leisure often cultivated the method of quiet sitting.

, on the advice of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he changed to the practice of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate and was quite diligent. The following summer he happened to catch a cold and lay weary in bed. Wang went to visit him and urged him to go to the outskirts of the city, the renowned Yunqi Monastery, to rest and recover while listening to the lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and accompanied him there. Returning after ten days, Wang visited again and found him suffering from diarrhea as well. He urged him, saying: You are a physician and can diagnose and treat yourself, but now that the illness has come to this, I fear your understanding and judgment may be wanting in accuracy; why not summon another physician for a consultation, so that you may recover sooner? The layman said: No, no. After you went to hear the sutra, there was one night when I saw Amitabha Buddha in a dream, and I joyfully made obeisance. Just as I was prostrating with the five limbs to the ground, I saw the Great One in White, his body likewise tall, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing his robe might brush against me, he lifted the hem with his hand and floated gently past my side, his smile brimming with warmth. Observing his manner, he seemed about to receive me and lead me to the West; what need is there to summon another physician for a further diagnosis? Before long the illness grew worse; knowing his time had come, he entrusted Wang with inviting a bhikshu to his home to assist in recitation, and thus on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month, he passed away seated in lotus, reciting the Buddha’s name.

When Wang, on his behalf, invited the bhikshu to come and recite the Buddha’s name, the layman said of himself: I will surely depart tonight. Wang, half-doubting and half-believing, made an agreement with him, saying: At present, rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation is attested only by the auspicious signs at death; after rebirth in the West there is no other conclusive proof. If you attain rebirth in the West this time, you must come in person to report and prove the truth of it; remember this most earnestly. The layman said: How shall I report? Wang said: Have you not seen the record in the books of Que Gongze’s reporting after rebirth in the West? The layman said: That manner of reporting requires nothing less than the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I do it? I can only report through a dream. Wang said: That is fine too, so long as it proves it.

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Laymen records: “Que Gongze was a man of Hebei. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty he lived in Luoyang, his life leisured and joyful, free and unconstrained, and he regularly recited the Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma. After Que Gongze passed away, his friends held an assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery in Luoyang. When evening came and the sutra was being recited, a voice was suddenly heard in the air. The assembly looked up and saw a person whose form and countenance were bright and beautiful, who said: ‘I am Que Gongze. I have already been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and now, together with all the superior ones, I have come here to hear the sutra.’ Everyone in the hall saw this sight. There was a man named Wei Shidu who lived in Ji Commandery and was a disciple of Que Gongze; his mother often offered vegetarian meals to the monks. That same day, toward noon, a bowl suddenly descended from the air and landed right before Wei’s mother. Examining it closely, they saw that it was the very bowl Que Gongze had always used, and it was filled with rice whose fragrance filled the whole hall. Everyone who ate the rice from the bowl went seven days without hunger. The eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Daolin praised this event without end.”
[Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma] Translated by Dharmarakṣa in the Western Jin, it is the earliest translation of the Lotus Sutra.

After he passed away seated, in accordance with the Buddha’s rule he was placed in the coffin and then cremated, and his ashes were placed in a stupa. When all was done, it was already mid-June. Time flew like a galloping colt; in the blink of an eye July, August, and September had all passed, and there was no news at all. I secretly thought that the layman had not attained rebirth in the West, or that, having attained it, he was unwilling to communicate with us, so that the agreement to report back had not been fulfilled. But unexpectedly, on the last day of the eleventh month (the end of the eleventh lunar month), Wang, suffering from a toothache, lay resting in bed in broad daylight. In a daze, he saw the layman ascend the stairs and sit on a stool. (Original note: Because Wang recited the Buddha’s name, his bed was placed beside the Buddha hall upstairs.) His build was as before; he wore a half-new flat cap and clothes that seemed recently washed, all clean, with a radiance shining in. His expression was bright and lively, his face like a full moon, and his skin delicate and tender like a handsome boy of eight. Compared with the face full of whiskers, the fallen teeth and wrinkled face of his lifetime, he seemed another person entirely. Had Wang not been his most intimate friend, knowing him to the utmost, and moreover a childhood companion, he would almost have failed to recognize him. For such beauty of bearing was something the layman had never possessed in all his life.

At the sight, Wang was overjoyed and astonished beyond measure; in his incoherence he asked abruptly: “Ah! So you have truly been reborn in the West! Otherwise, how could you have such a bearing? You yourself do not know that your face is now completely that of a tender, handsome boy. In life you lost more than half your teeth, and I once invited you to Songzhu Ju to have them set — do you still remember?” The layman said: “Yes, yes. I have come specially to tell you and report.” Wang said: “The West is a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here, no easy place to reach, yet you have actually arrived.” He answered: “My having attained it is entirely through the power of faith and vows.” Wang said: “How could you get here?” He answered: “Very easily — with a single thought one is there; in time you will know it yourself. When one wishes to come, one looks toward the darkness; when one wishes to go, one looks toward the brightness; that is all.” Wang asked again: “Have you seen the Buddha?” He answered: “Not yet.” “Why could you not see him?” “My meritorious practice is too shallow; I have not been born into the pond of seven jewels.” “If not born into the pond of seven jewels, where were you born?” The layman sighed deeply: “Alas, the place where I was born is merely the ground of the West. Ah, I suppose it counts as the borderland.”
